summary: This Standards Track document extends the RPSL inetnum: class to refer to prefixlen files, which are CSV files stating end-site prefix lengths. It also describes an optional way to authenticate those files with the RPKI.

eli5.summary: A neighborhood posts a list saying how big a lot each house gets, with an optional stamp proving the list is real.

questions: what is an end-site prefix length
how to publish prefixlen in inetnum
subtitle: A standard way for networks to publish how big a slice of address space each customer gets, with optional RPKI signing.

tldr.problem: Content providers have no easy way to know the end-site prefix size of someone using their service. Guessing wrong causes overblocking, shared rate limits, or bloated blocklists and geolocation databases.
tldr.mechanism: Operators publish a CSV prefixlen file giving the end-site prefix length (and any CGN end-site count) per prefix, and point to it from an inetnum: object using a prefixlen: attribute or a remarks: line. The file can carry an optional RPKI-based CMS signature.
tldr.outcome: Consumers can find and read the data in a defined way and can verify who published it when it is signed. Signing is optional, and the RFC warns that publishers can still publish wrong data.

facts.label: Fetch protocol
facts.value: HTTPS (FTP must not be used for bulk download)

today: RFC 9977 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated. As of November 2025, the RIPE NCC database had implemented the prefixlen: attribute, and other registrants use remarks:.

sections.title: Why End-Site Prefix Lengths Matter
sections.content:
ISPs hand their users addresses or whole prefixes, and cloud providers give each customer, for example a virtual machine, a prefix of a specific size. As a result, many different end-site prefix lengths exist on the Internet, and there is currently no easy way for a content provider to learn the size for someone reaching its service.

The RFC names three places where this hurts. Blocklisting and throttling: in IPv6, blocking at /48 or /56 can overblock, while blocking at /64, /96 or /128 fills the blocklist quickly and may unblock users with temporary addresses. Rate limiting and CAPTCHAs: neighbours in the same /48 or /56 even though the ISP hands out /64s hit shared limits. Geolocation: aggregating too much mixes clients in different places, and aggregating too little fills the database with needless entries.
sections.eli5: If a website cannot tell whether a whole street or just one house is knocking, it may lock out the wrong people. A published list of lot sizes tells it who is who.

sections.title: The prefixlen File
sections.content:
A prefixlen file is a CSV file in UTF-8 text. Lines end with CRLF, blank lines are ignored, and anything from a hash character to the end of the line is a comment. Each line has exactly three fields, so exactly two commas: the prefix, the end-site prefix length within it, and the number of end-sites for networks using Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) or proxies. The first field must not be empty. If both the second and third fields are empty, the publisher does not want to disclose any prefix length information.

An ISP giving each customer a /56 of 2001:db8::/32 and a single IPv4 address from 192.0.2.0/24 writes the lines shown in the figure. A third field of 1 means no CGN or proxies, the same as leaving it empty. For CGN, the third field counts end-sites at the length in the second field: 192.0.2.0/24,26,1000 means 1000 CGN end-sites in each of the four /26 sub-prefixes.

Files can contain sub-prefixes of a parent prefix, so consumers must use longest prefix matching. An entry with both fields empty, such as 192.0.2.0/28,,, discards any prefix length information from covering prefixes for that sub-prefix.
sections.eli5: Each line says: in this block of addresses, every house gets a lot this big, and this many families share one house if there is sharing. A more specific line beats a general one.

sections.title: Processing the Data
sections.content:
Multiple entries with exactly the same prefix are an error. Publishers MUST ensure there is one and only one entry per prefix, and consumers SHOULD log repeats. When a consumer meets an erroneous entry, it MUST skip it, log the error and continue with the rest.

Files from large providers can contain millions of entries. When reading a file, one MUST ignore data outside the address range of the referring inetnum: object, so that nobody imports data about ranges they do not control. If a prefixlen file is fetched, other prefix length information from the inetnum: must be ignored.
sections.eli5: If a list says two different things about the same street, the reader skips that line and makes a note. It also ignores lines about streets the list owner does not own.

sections.title: Finding the File Through inetnum:
sections.content:
The RFC builds on the RPSL inetnum: database class, which describes an IP address range; wherever inetnum: appears, inet6num: is assumed too. The ideal is a new prefixlen: attribute. Where a registry has not implemented it, the RFC defines a remarks: line of the form remarks: Prefixlen <URL>, where the word Prefixlen is case-sensitive and the HTTPS URL refers to a single prefixlen file. If both forms exist, prefixlen: wins, and consumers MUST understand both until all registries and registrants have migrated.

Fetching follows the most specific inetnum: object that has a prefixlen reference. In the RFC's example, a lookup for 192.0.2.0/29 must ignore the file referenced by the covering 192.0.2.0/24 object and use the one referenced by 192.0.2.0/26.

For bulk collection, registries' bulk-download services SHOULD be used over HTTPS, and FTP MUST NOT be used. Fetchers MUST NOT do frequent real-time lookups, MUST honor HTTP Expires or Cache-Control headers, and absent such headers SHOULD NOT fetch more often than weekly.
sections.eli5: The registry's phone book entry for a block of addresses has a note saying where to find that block's lot-size list. If a smaller block has its own note, use that one.

sections.title: Optional RPKI Signatures
sections.content:
Registry data is sometimes weakly authenticated, so the RFC defines an optional authenticator based on the RPKI signed object template. A single authenticator MAY be appended to a prefixlen file. It is a detached CMS signature over the canonicalized file text, DER-encoded and Base64-encoded, made with the key of an RPKI certificate that covers the file's address range.

The signing certificate MUST cover every prefix in the file, MUST NOT contain the AS Identifier Delegation extension, and MUST NOT use inherit in its IP Address Delegation extension. The CA MUST create a new End Entity certificate for each signing, and the key SHOULD sign only one prefixlen file. Validation checks that key identifiers match, the signer's certificate is on the current manifest, the certification path is valid, the CMS signature verifies, the content type OID is 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.57, and the resources cover the file. All steps must succeed.

The signature sits at the end of the file as hash-prefixed comment lines between RPKI Signature: and End Signature: markers, and is not covered by the signature itself. A signed file MUST be preferred over an unsigned one for the same range, and a signed file cannot be referenced by multiple inetnum: objects.
sections.eli5: The owner can sign the list with a special pen that only the real owner of the addresses has. Anyone can then check that the signature is genuine.

sections.title: Operations and Implementation Status
sections.content:
Prefixlen files MUST be published and fetched over HTTPS. Operators coordinate with their RIR, NIR or provider LIR to create the inetnum: objects. Harvesting and republishing aggregated prefixlen data outside the RPSL model SHOULD be avoided, because it can let more specifics from one party affect another and prevents readers from running the checks above.

As of November 2025, the prefixlen: attribute has been implemented by the RIPE NCC database. Other registrants use remarks:. ARIN's data is not the same RPSL as the other registries, so its NetRange or ip network key is treated as inetnum and its Comment as remarks.
sections.eli5: Publishing the list means asking your address registry to add the note. Today one registry has a special field for it, and the others use a plain comment line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Consumers SHOULD fetch and process the data themselves, since using datasets produced by a third party places significant trust in that party. Weakly authenticated registries allow spoofed inetnum: objects that point to malicious files. The RFC also describes an attack on signed files: someone could publish an unsigned, equal or narrower inetnum: in a weakly authorized registry and abuse the rule that the most specific object wins. Mandatory signatures would stop this, but the RFC says that is not happening anytime soon.

Published data can also be wrong, by mistake or on purpose: a very specific size such as /128 over large IPv6 blocks to overflow consumers' storage, false CGN claims to avoid throttling, fake small allocations, or files with millions or billions of entries. Disclosing end-site boundaries could also help attackers aim DDoS traffic or IPv6 scanning. Registries already throttle fetchers, and prefixlen servers will likely need similar defenses.
sections.eli5: A list can be forged or can lie, so a careful reader checks where it came from and does not blindly believe every line.
